warmup.title: Warm-up
warmup.prompt: Three easy minutes to get your voice moving. Keep everything gentle and quiet.

steps.label: Lip trills
steps.how: Let your lips flutter on a breath, like a motorboat, sliding up and down a little. Hold your cheeks lightly if they won’t buzz.

steps.label: Hum on “mm”
steps.how: Hum with your lips closed, gliding gently around your speaking pitch. You should feel a buzz on your lips.

steps.label: “ng” slides
steps.how: Hum “ng”, as at the end of “sing”, and slide up and back down. Only as far as is easy.

cooldown.title: Cool-down
cooldown.prompt: A minute to settle your voice after practice.

steps.label: Downward sighs
steps.how: Sigh gently on “hmm”, gliding from a comfortable middle note down to low.

steps.label: Easy hum
steps.how: Hum quietly at a relaxed, low-ish pitch. Let your jaw and shoulders drop.

units.title: Setup
units.summary: How practice works, how to keep your voice safe, and your starting point.

exercises.title: Many small changes
body: A voice is shaped by several things at once: pitch, brightness (resonance), weight and melody. No single number decides how a voice comes across, so NewVoice trains them one at a time and then together.
Every target is measured against your own starting point and the goal you chose, and rises in small steps. There is no pass or fail for your voice, only practice.

exercises.title: Keeping your voice safe
body: Each session starts with a three-minute warm-up and ends with a short cool-down. Sessions stop at about 20 minutes, with at most an hour a day. Short sessions spread through the week build a voice better than long ones.
Stop if anything hurts, your throat feels raw, you sound hoarse afterwards, or your voice cuts out. The stop button is on every voice exercise.
Nothing is rewarded above the top of your comfortable range.

exercises.title: Why you’re here
exercises.prompt: Optional. Only you can read this; it stays on this phone.
questions: What would you like your voice to do for you?

exercises.title: Record your starting point
body: Six short recordings in your everyday voice: three held vowels, a slide, a few sentences and 30 seconds of talking. Everything after this is measured against them.
It takes about five minutes. Find a quiet spot.

units.title: Hearing
units.summary: Train your ear to hear pitch, brightness and weight before you change them.

exercises.title: Which is higher?
exercises.prompt: You’ll hear two sounds. Pick the higher one. The differences get smaller as you go.

exercises.title: Brightness is not pitch
body: Two sounds can have the same pitch and still differ: one sounds smaller and brighter, the other bigger and darker. That is resonance, the shape of the space your voice passes through.
In these pairs the pitch stays the same. Listen for size.

exercises.title: Which is brighter?
exercises.prompt: Same pitch, different size. Pick the brighter, smaller-sounding one.

exercises.title: Which is lighter?
exercises.prompt: Same pitch, same vowel. One has more buzz and heft. Pick the lighter one.

exercises.title: Odd one out
exercises.prompt: Three sounds; two are the same. Pick the one that is brighter or darker than the others.

exercises.title: Brightness check
exercises.prompt: Ten pairs at a set difference. Pick the brighter one each time.

units.title: Pitch
units.summary: Find your comfortable range and land on a target note.

exercises.title: Easy, not far
body: Range grows slowly, over weeks. In each session, only go as high and as low as feels easy. The top of your comfortable range is a limit the app never rewards you for passing.

exercises.title: Slide up and down
exercises.prompt: On “ng”, slide from low to high and back, as far as is easy. Watch the line move.

exercises.title: Hum to the tone
exercises.prompt: Listen to the tone, then hum it. Keep the dot on the line for a moment.

exercises.title: Mm-hm at your target
exercises.prompt: Say a light, friendly “mm-hm?” as if agreeing with a friend. Keep the dot in the band.

exercises.title: Land on the note
exercises.prompt: Ten notes in a voice-like tone. Hum or say “mm-hm” on each and hold it.

units.title: Light weight
units.summary: Let your voice get lighter, using slides and small, friendly sounds.

exercises.title: Heavy and light
body: Weight is how heavy or buzzy a voice sounds. Going higher usually makes a voice lighter, and going lower makes it heavier, which is why pitch and weight are trained together.
The weight number in NewVoice is an estimate from the sound’s spectrum, compared with your own starting point. Treat it as a hint, not a measurement of how you sound to others.
Light is not breathy. Don’t add air to hide weight: it tires the voice and is hard to undo.

exercises.title: Slide up, let it lighten
exercises.prompt: On “oo”, slide up from a relaxed middle note and let the sound get lighter as it rises. Stop well before anything feels tight.

exercises.title: Small, friendly sounds
exercises.prompt: Say these the way you’d talk to a puppy: light and easy. Keep the dot in the band.

exercises.title: Keep it light on the way down
exercises.prompt: Start light and high-ish on “oo”, then slide down slowly, keeping the light quality. Stop where it starts to get heavy.

exercises.title: Feel the difference
exercises.prompt: Once only: slide down and let the voice get heavier, then slide back up without lightening. This is to feel weight, not to practise it.

exercises.title: Light phrases
exercises.prompt: Say each phrase lightly, at your target. This checkpoint passes after three separate sessions.

units.title: Size
units.summary: Make the space your voice passes through smaller, using whispers.

exercises.title: Why whisper
body: A whisper has no pitch, so you can change size without pitch getting in the way. It is also quiet enough to practise almost anywhere.
Whisper softly. A forced whisper is harder on the voice than speaking.

exercises.title: Your ordinary whisper
exercises.prompt: Whisper a long “ee” the way you normally would, for about 4 seconds. This is your reference for the next lessons.

exercises.title: Slide the whisper up
exercises.prompt: Whisper “ee” and slide it up like a tiny siren. Make the bar climb.

exercises.title: Small dog panting
exercises.prompt: Pant softly like a big dog, then like a small dog. Hold the small-dog shape and whisper “hee”.

exercises.title: Feel the rise
body: Put a fingertip lightly on your throat and swallow: you’ll feel the bump rise and fall. Next time, let it rise just a little and stay there while you breathe. Never hold it with force.

exercises.title: Smaller and brighter
exercises.prompt: Whisper “ee” with the small-dog shape and hold it for about 4 seconds.

units.title: Brightness
units.summary: Brighten each vowel with your tongue and lips.

exercises.title: Move the dot right
body: Brightness follows where your tongue sits and the shape of your lips. A forward tongue and slightly spread lips brighten a vowel; a pulled-back tongue and rounded lips darken it.
Use the chart as your guide: make the dot move right and up the brightness scale.

exercises.title: Bright “ee”
exercises.prompt: Say each word with your tongue forward, as if smiling slightly. Keep the brightness dot in the band.

exercises.title: Rounded, then spread
exercises.prompt: Read the line once with rounded lips, then once with lips gently spread. Watch brightness change.

exercises.title: Climb the ladder
exercises.prompt: Hold each vowel for about two seconds and brighten it. Keep your pitch where it is comfortable.

exercises.title: Six bright vowels
exercises.prompt: Hold each vowel for about two seconds, as bright as is comfortable. Six of the seven need to reach your target.

units.title: Combine
units.summary: Hold pitch, lightness and brightness together, from a vowel to words.

exercises.title: Hold “ee”
exercises.prompt: Find your target on a light, bright “ee” and hold it. Keep both dots in their bands.

exercises.title: Lock and speak
exercises.prompt: Keep the same setting from “ee” and say each word.

exercises.title: Twenty words
exercises.prompt: Say each word with your target pitch and brightness. Aim to stay in the bands most of the time.

units.title: Melody
units.summary: Use more of your range in each phrase, if that’s a style you want.

exercises.title: A style choice
body: Listeners tend to hear more upward movement and a wider range within each phrase as lighter and more expressive. Research also shows people of every gender use plenty of different melodies, so this is a style to have available, not a rule.

exercises.title: Read it your usual way
exercises.prompt: Read these lines in your usual way, at your target pitch. This is your reference for the next lessons.

exercises.title: Let it rise
exercises.prompt: Let each question lift at the end. Watch the end of the line curve up.

exercises.title: Statements and questions
exercises.prompt: Read each line with a little more movement than your usual way. Let questions rise.
lines: We should go to the sea.

units.title: Articulate
units.summary: Lighter consonants, and keeping your voice in laughs and little sounds.

exercises.title: Forward and light
body: Consonants made lightly at the front of the mouth help keep vowels bright. Touch, don’t press: the tip of the tongue taps, the lips meet softly.
The evidence that consonants alone change how a voice is heard is weak, so treat this as polish.

exercises.title: Tip of the tongue
exercises.prompt: Read lightly, tapping each consonant with the tip of your tongue. Keep your pitch in the band.

exercises.title: Oops!
exercises.prompt: These sounds slip back to an old setting unless practised. Find your target on “mm-hm”, then make each sound.
exercises.question: How close to your target did that feel?

exercises.title: Across the room
exercises.prompt: Call out as if to someone across a room, without shouting. Loudness pulls voices toward weight, so keep it light.
exercises.question: How close to your target did that feel?

exercises.title: Sounds in your voice
exercises.prompt: Make each sound in your target voice, then rate it. Your rating and your pitch both count.
exercises.question: How close to your target did that feel?

units.title: Carryover
units.summary: From reading to talking freely, keeping your new setting.

exercises.title: A short passage
exercises.prompt: Read the passage at your target, at a relaxed pace.
lines: The blue spot is on the key again.
How hard did he hit him?
We were away a year ago.
Peter will keep at the peak.

exercises.title: Thirty seconds
exercises.prompt: Talk for 30 seconds about one of these, in your target voice.
prompts: How to make a cup of tea.

exercises.title: Talk for a minute
exercises.prompt: Talk for a minute. This checkpoint passes when your talking pitch stays in your zone, steadily, across three sessions.
prompts: A skill you’d like to learn.

units.title: Life
units.summary: Phone calls, loud rooms, feelings, and the world outside.

exercises.title: On the phone
body: Phone lines cut off the lowest and highest parts of a voice, so brightness and lightness carry more of the message there. A bright, light setting matters more on a call than pitch does.

exercises.title: Answer the phone
exercises.prompt: Read as if answering a call. Hold the phone as you would on a call.
lines: Sorry, could you say that again?

exercises.title: Projecting
exercises.prompt: Speak up as in a noisy café. Add brightness, not weight.
lines: Can I get a large tea, please?

exercises.title: With feeling
exercises.prompt: Read each line with the feeling in brackets, staying in your setting.

exercises.title: A voice in the wild
exercises.prompt: Pick one when you feel ready. There’s no deadline, and it’s fine to choose an easy one.
ideas: Order a drink at a café.
Make a short phone call, like booking an appointment.
Say hello to a neighbour or shop assistant.
Leave a voice message for a friend.

exercises.title: Looking back
exercises.prompt: Optional. Only you can read this.
questions: What felt easier than you expected?
